Installation and setup

Source: vignettes/example5.Rmd
example5.Rmd

bayesnec fits its models with brms (Bürkner 2017; Bürkner 2018), which passes them to Stan (https://mc-stan.org/). Stan does not interpret a model; instead, each model is translated into C++ and compiled into a program, and that program is run. A C++ toolchain is therefore required to fit any model at all, and compilation is also the reason the first fit of a session takes longer than the fits after it.

brms samples through either of two back ends (i.e. the R packages through which it compiles and runs the Stan program). rstan (Stan Development Team 2025) is installed as a dependency of brms whether or not it is used as the sampler, so it is present on any machine that can load brms. However, this package’s own vignettes are built with cmdstanr, which is not on CRAN and is not in the dependency list of bayesnec, and which is selected with options(brms.backend = "cmdstanr"). We describe the installation of cmdstanr below, and the rstan route is documented by the Stan project (https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/wiki/RStan-Getting-Started).

Software requirements

Software Purpose
R the language the package runs in
A C++ toolchain compiles each model before it is fitted
CmdStan the sampler that runs the compiled model

Of these, the toolchain is the component that differs between operating systems (Rtools on Windows, the Xcode Command Line Tools on macOS, and the standard build tools on Linux), and it is also the component that most often fails.

Route by operating system

Windows requires the most care, and is described in its own section below. Historically, the difficulties of running Stan on Windows came from rstan, which requires matched versions of several compiled packages. cmdstanr avoids most of these, and the difficulties that remain concern the toolchain and the installation path.

Linux requires the least care, because the build tools of a current distribution are already what Stan requires, and the default installation path raises none of the problems described in the Windows section.

These instructions have not been verified on macOS, so for macOS we point to the instructions maintained by the projects themselves.

Whether an installation works is determined by the check in the Verification section, regardless of which of these routes was followed.

Windows

R and Rtools

Install R first (from https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/base/), and then the Rtools that matches it (from https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/). Accept the default installation location for each.

Rtools is versioned against the minor version of R, and CRAN’s Rtools page lists which Rtools goes with which R. A mismatch between them is the most common single cause of a failed setup, so install R first and read that page, instead of reusing an Rtools already on the machine.

cmdstanr::check_cmdstan_toolchain() names the Rtools version that cmdstanr is looking for, and that is the version to install. The function becomes available once cmdstanr has been installed (see the next section). Under cmdstanr 0.9.0 and R 4.6.1, for example, the message is

Rtools45 was not found but is required to run CmdStan with R version 4.6.1.
Please install Rtools45 and run cmdstanr::check_cmdstan_toolchain().

The version cmdstanr looks for is fixed in the installed cmdstanr and is not read from CRAN, so it may differ from the Rtools that CRAN pairs with that version of R. That case is described under Recurring problems on Windows below.

R packages

cmdstanr is not on CRAN, so it is installed from the Stan project’s own repository:

install.packages("cmdstanr",
                 repos = c("https://stan-dev.r-universe.dev",
                           getOption("repos")))

bayesnec and the remaining packages are installed from CRAN, and installing bayesnec also installs brms:

install.packages("bayesnec")

The CmdStan installation

Before installing CmdStan, confirm that the compiler is configured. On a current Rtools this check passes without making any change, and fix = TRUE repairs the problems it can, instead of only reporting them.

cmdstanr::check_cmdstan_toolchain(fix = TRUE)

Then install CmdStan with the code below, which sets three things, each of which has been observed to stop a fresh installation on Windows.

dir.create("C:/cmdstan")           # install_cmdstan() does not create it
options(timeout = 1800)            # R's default of 60 seconds is too short
cmdstanr::install_cmdstan(dir = "C:/cmdstan")

The directory has to exist before install_cmdstan() is called, because the function does not create it and instead stops with Assertion on 'dir' failed: Directory 'C:/cmdstan' does not exist.

The download needs a longer timeout than R’s default. The CmdStan archive is about 49 MB, and its download is governed by options(timeout), not by the timeout argument of install_cmdstan(). When this was measured on a connection delivering about 500 KB/s, the download failed with Download of CmdStan failed with error at the default timeout, and completed in 4.9 minutes at timeout = 1800 with nothing else changed. We recommend setting the timeout in any case, because it has no effect where the download would have completed anyway.

The installation path has to be a plain one. The default location is inside the home directory, and on many Windows machines (particularly those managed by an employer) that directory is synchronised by OneDrive, where the CmdStan build fails. The build also fails where the path contains a space or a character outside the standard English alphabet, as the home directory does when the Windows user name contains one. C:/cmdstan avoids all three problems, although installing there instead of in the default location requires two things in return: the CMDSTAN variable described below, and dir = "C:/cmdstan" in any later call to install_cmdstan().

Because C:/cmdstan is not the default location, R has to be told where to find it in each later session, and cmdstanr reads this setting from an environment variable, not from an option. To set it, run usethis::edit_r_environ() (or open .Renviron in your home directory), add the line below, and restart R. Without this line, cmdstanr shows CmdStan as not installed in each new session, and the path has to be set by hand in each one.

CMDSTAN=C:/cmdstan

R reads .Renviron only when it starts, which is why the edit takes effect in the next session and not in the current one. The variable is the only setting cmdstanr reads for this purpose: in cmdstanr 0.9.0, cmdstanr:::cmdstanr_initialize() takes the path from Sys.getenv("CMDSTAN") where that is set and from ~/.cmdstan otherwise, and no option sets it.

The version number is not needed in the variable. Where CMDSTAN names a directory that is not itself an installation (such as C:/cmdstan), cmdstanr takes the newest cmdstan-* installation inside it, so the line above continues to work after the next CmdStan upgrade without being edited. Setting the path by hand, however, does need the version number, and this difference is a likely source of error. cmdstanr::set_cmdstan_path() takes the path as given, so it has to be called as set_cmdstan_path("C:/cmdstan/cmdstan-2.39.0"). Given the parent directory instead, it sets the path to that directory, the version read by cmdstan_version() is left at NULL, and it gives the warning

Can't find CmdStan makefile to detect version number. Path may not point to valid installation.

The back end is set by an option, not by an environment variable, so on all platforms it belongs in .Rprofile, where it does not have to be set again in each session:

options(brms.backend = "cmdstanr")

Recurring problems on Windows

A partly built CmdStan directory

Where install_cmdstan() fails, run it again with these arguments.

cmdstanr::install_cmdstan(overwrite = TRUE, quiet = FALSE, dir = "C:/cmdstan")

Of these arguments, overwrite = TRUE is the important one. An attempt that fails partway through the build results in a partly built directory, and a second attempt without overwrite declines to replace it, giving an error that resembles the first one. quiet = FALSE only prints more of the build output, which is useful because the default output is truncated and does not identify the stage that failed.

Chains that do not start after an Rtools upgrade

A model compiles, but cmdstanr then gives the message No chains finished successfully, which names no cause and no file. This typically follows a change to Rtools after CmdStan was installed. CmdStan builds its own tbb.dll, linked against the toolchain that built it, so a CmdStan built under Rtools44 requires libraries that Rtools45 does not provide; the model still compiles, but each chain then exits immediately with STATUS_DLL_NOT_FOUND. Rebuilding CmdStan resolves the problem.

cmdstanr::install_cmdstan(overwrite = TRUE, dir = "C:/cmdstan")

Anyone who upgrades R and Rtools after installing CmdStan will encounter this.

The cmdstanr version and the Rtools it expects

Rtools is installed, but cmdstanr gives a message that it is missing. This is because cmdstanr chooses which Rtools to look for from the R version, and that choice is fixed in the installed cmdstanr. In 0.9.0, cmdstanr:::rtools4x_version() returns Rtools44 for R 4.4.x and Rtools45 for all versions of R from 4.5 onward, which is why R 4.6.1 is sent to Rtools45. Version 0.8.0 sent all versions from R 4.4 onward to Rtools44, so an older cmdstanr installed beside the Rtools that CRAN pairs with R 4.5.x searches for a toolchain that was never installed.

Install cmdstanr 0.9.0 or later (as supplied by the r-universe repository above), and install the Rtools named by check_cmdstan_toolchain() instead of the one inferred from the R version.

Slow compilation

Windows Defender inspects each newly compiled program, so a compile that would otherwise take under a minute may take several. Where the machine’s policy allows, excluding the CmdStan directory from real-time scanning resolves this.

Compilation blocked by policy

Some managed machines prevent a newly compiled program from running at all. The block results from the machine’s policy and not from a problem in the configuration. It cannot be worked around from within R, and resolving it requires whoever administers the machine.

macOS

These steps have not been verified on macOS. They point to the upstream instructions maintained by the projects themselves, and whether the installation works is established by the check in the Verification section.

  1. Install R from https://cran.r-project.org/bin/macosx/, choosing the build for your processor (the Apple Silicon and Intel builds differ).
  2. Install the Xcode Command Line Tools by running xcode-select --install in Terminal. Some packages also require gfortran, and the current requirement is given on CRAN’s macOS tools page.
  3. Install the R packages as described in the Windows section above.
  4. Follow the CmdStanR getting-started vignette (https://mc-stan.org/cmdstanr/articles/cmdstanr.html) for check_cmdstan_toolchain() and install_cmdstan(). The default installation path causes no difficulty on macOS, so dir need not be set, and no CMDSTAN variable is needed either.
  5. Put options(brms.backend = "cmdstanr") in .Rprofile, as in the Windows section.

Linux

Install R through the distribution’s package manager or from CRAN, together with the standard build tools (build-essential on Debian and Ubuntu, or the equivalent development group on other distributions). After installing the R packages as described in the Windows section, run cmdstanr::check_cmdstan_toolchain() and then cmdstanr::install_cmdstan(). As on macOS, the default path causes no difficulty, so no CMDSTAN variable is needed, and options(brms.backend = "cmdstanr") belongs in .Rprofile as it does on Windows.

Verification

The installation is verified with two checks. Run them in order, because the first inspects the toolchain and the second uses it.

cmdstanr::check_cmdstan_toolchain()
cmdstanr::cmdstan_version()

On a configured toolchain, check_cmdstan_toolchain() gives the message

The C++ toolchain required for CmdStan is setup properly!

and cmdstan_version() returns the version string of the installation that R is using. An error from either function indicates a problem with the toolchain or the path, and nothing below will work until it is resolved.

The second check fits a model. It is the decisive check, because it exercises the whole path (bnec() calls brms::brm(), brm() writes a Stan program, CmdStan compiles it, and the compiled program samples).

library(bayesnec)
data(nec_data)

options(brms.backend = "cmdstanr")
set.seed(333)
fit <- bnec(y ~ crf(x, model = "nec4param"), data = nec_data,
            family = Beta(link = "identity"), chains = 2, seed = 333)
summary(fit)

A successful run compiles one Stan program, prints the sampling progress of two chains, and returns an object of class bayesnecfit. Its summary() shows the four parameters of the nec4param equation (bot, top, beta and nec), each with an Rhat near 1.00. These are followed by a Further Distributional Parameters block containing phi (the precision of the Beta response), then the NEC estimate with its credible interval, and then a Bayesian R-squared. Two chains are enough to show that the toolchain works. An analysis, however, should use the brms default of four chains, which the other vignettes take.

Once this fit returns, the modelling vignettes can be followed, beginning with Single model usage.

Provenance

The Windows failures described above, and the measurements quoted with them (the 49 MB archive, the download that failed at R’s default timeout and completed in 4.9 minutes at timeout = 1800, the OneDrive build failure, and the tbb.dll linked against a superseded Rtools), are taken from the software setup module of the concentration-response modelling course (https://github.com/open-AIMS/cr_modelling_training, commit 9d05595). That module records what was observed on fresh Windows machines during 2026, and these are the course’s measurements, not this package’s.

All statements here about cmdstanr behaviour were read from cmdstanr 0.9.0 under R 4.6.1, and none of them is a course measurement. They are: the environment variable read by cmdstanr:::cmdstanr_initialize(), and its fallback to ~/.cmdstan; the resolution of a CMDSTAN directory that is not itself an installation to the newest cmdstan-* inside it, and the absence of that resolution from set_cmdstan_path(); the Rtools version returned by cmdstanr:::rtools4x_version(); the text of three of the messages quoted above (i.e. the toolchain success, the missing Rtools, and the directory assertion); the assertion by install_cmdstan() that a supplied directory exists, instead of creating it; the forwarding of fix = TRUE by check_cmdstan_toolchain() to the branch that repairs problems instead of only reporting them; and the timeout argument being passed to build_cmdstan() and build_example(), while the download runs through utils::download.file() and so honours options(timeout).

The Linux route was checked on 2026-09-11 by running the course’s verification script end to end, with R 4.6.1, brms 2.23.0, cmdstanr 0.9.0 and CmdStan 2.39.0. This check has two limitations: it was run under WSL2 Debian and not on a native installation, and the machine was already configured, so it confirms that the end state works but does not test the instructions for reaching it.
